title: A Capitalist in North Korea: My Seven Years in the Hermit Kingdom
author: Felix Abt
target_audience: Readers interested in North Korean society and business
Business professionals seeking insight into challenging markets
Historians and students of modern East Asia
General readers intrigued by rare inside accounts of North Korea
core_themes: Daily life and business in North Korea under dictatorship
Practical and ethical dilemmas of entrepreneurship in a closed economy
Humanizing the North Korean people beyond propaganda
Challenges of international sanctions and political tension
primary_purpose: To shed light on the realities of living and doing business in North Korea from an outsider’s perspective, offering unique insights into the country’s economic, social, and human landscape through first-hand experience.

structure_format.organization: Chronological recounting of Felix Abt’s seven-year tenure in North Korea with thematic chapters on business, culture, and politics
features: Reflections on business ethics under a repressive regime
Photographs and documentation of everyday life

key_concepts_lessons: North Korea’s people are resilient, resourceful, and more diverse than often depicted.
Running a business in North Korea requires navigating complex bureaucracy, limited resources, and unpredictable politics.
Adaptability, patience, and cultural sensitivity are essential for any foreigner undertaking work in extreme environments.
International perceptions of North Korea often differ from the nuanced reality experienced day-to-day.
Ethical dilemmas are ever-present when profits and survival hinge on cooperation with an autocratic government.
notable_features: One of the few detailed Western memoirs of living and working in North Korea
First-hand accounts of starting and managing legitimate businesses under sanctions
Analysis of how economic opportunities and restrictions shape ordinary life
Photographic documentation of rarely seen settings inside North Korea
cultural_historical_context: Set during the 2000s, a period of limited diplomatic engagement, increasing sanctions, and ongoing tension between North Korea and the international community. The book provides valuable on-the-ground perspective during an era when the country remained largely inaccessible to outsiders.
reception_impact: Received as a rare, credible account of North Korean life by an expatriate
Appreciated for its humanizing portrayal of North Koreans beyond stereotypes
Cited in discussions and analysis of North Korean external business relations
Praised for its balance, avoiding both sensationalism and naiveté
comparable_titles: Nothing to Envy: Ordinary Lives in North Korea by Barbara Demick
The Aquariums of Pyongyang by Kang Chol-Hwan
Without You, There Is No Us by Suki Kim
Under the Same Sky: From Starvation in North Korea to Salvation in America by Joseph Kim
